title: The Scattered Households argued against Montanism
dates: The second century, while the New Prophecy was new
datesNote: No old source gives a year for the meetings. The anonymous writer says Montanus began when Gratus was proconsul of Asia, and gives no year. He wrote more than thirteen years after Maximilla's death.
place: The Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey
shortDescription: In the Roman province of Asia, the faithful met often, in many places, to examine the sayings of the New Prophecy's prophets. They judged the sayings profane, put the prophets' followers out of the church and barred them from communion.

directLine.confidenceInWords: Documented: a writer of the time says it happened, and Eusebius copied his words.

text: Eusebius of Caesarea quotes a writer of about 192 whose name is lost. He says the faithful of Asia met many times to test what the prophets of Phrygia taught. They found it to be heresy, and cut those who held it off from communion. Apolinarius, bishop of Hierapolis, also wrote against the Phrygians.

timeline.when: When Gratus was proconsul of Asia
timeline.headline: Prophets appear in Phrygia
timeline.witness: The anonymous writer against them, a presbyter, as Eusebius copied him

lines.text: At Ardabau, a village of Mysia on the border of Phrygia, a recent convert named Montanus falls into what the writer calls a frenzy and ecstasy, and prophesies against the custom handed down in the church.
Two women also prophesy in the same way. The spirit, the writer says, taught them to revile the whole church, because the church gave it neither honor nor entrance.

timeline.headline: The churches of Asia test the prophets and cast them out
timeline.witness: The anonymous writer, as Eusebius copied him

lines.text: The faithful of Asia meet often, in many places, examine the new sayings, pronounce them profane and reject the heresy. Its followers are expelled from the church and barred from communion.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History V.16.10, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 29721-29738; second English, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml line 11308

lines.text: Bishops try to refute the spirit in Maximilla, among them Zoticus of Comana and Julian of Apamea, and her followers stop them.
The prophets' side calls their opponents slayers of the prophets, for refusing prophets they say the Lord promised to send.

lines.when: while Montanus "was then laying the foundations of his error"
lines.text: Apolinarius, bishop of Hierapolis, writes against the heresy of the Phrygians.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History IV.27, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 26111-26112, 26147-26150; V.19.2, lines 30561-30562
lines.note: Eusebius's own placing of the writings.

timeline.when: After Maximilla's death, to Eusebius's day
timeline.headline: The case against them written down and passed on

lines.text: The anonymous writer, a presbyter, disputes against the prophets for many days in the church at Ancyra in Galatia.

lines.when: more than thirteen years after Maximilla's death
lines.text: He writes his books against them for Avircius Marcellus.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History V.16.3 and V.16.19, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 29455-29456, 29886-29888

lines.text: Serapion, bishop of Antioch, sends on the writings of Apolinarius against the New Prophecy.
Eusebius copies the anonymous writer's account into his Church History.

stories.title: Zoticus Tries to Silence Maximilla’s Spirit

whatPassed: A judgment: the faithful of Asia examined the prophets' sayings, pronounced them profane and rejected them as heresy (HE V.16.10, lines 29721-29736).
A break in fellowship: those who held the sayings were expelled from the church and barred from communion, shut out of its shared meal (lines 29736-29738).
Writings against them: Apolinarius of Hierapolis wrote against the heresy of the Phrygians (HE IV.27, lines 26111-26112), and the anonymous writer's books carried the case on (lines 29455-29456).
From the other side, a charge in return: the prophets' side called their opponents slayers of the prophets (HE V.16.12, lines 29745-29754).

legacyAndToday: The case against them was kept because Eusebius copied it into his Church History (HE V.16, lines 29432-29451).
Jerome later drew on the same writers: Apollonius, he says, wrote "a notable and lengthy volume" against Montanus, Prisca and Maximilla (NPNF 2.3, lines 40300-40302).
uncertain: When the meetings were held, and where. The anonymous writer gives neither a year nor a town for them.
What exactly the meetings condemned. The writer does not list the sayings. What his own account faults is the manner: frenzy and ecstasy against the church's custom.
Who Apolinarius's writings were sent to, and whether they were books or letters. Eusebius says only that he wrote them.
